| [NOTE-1245](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1245.md) | Preregistered Replication and Extension of "Moral Hypocrisy: Social Groups and the Flexibility of Virtue" | Two preregistered online experiments (Prolific, US). Neither replicated Valdesolo and DeSteno's intergroup moral hypocrisy (the original N was 76 and d was 1.11); the minimal-group contrast is statistically equivalent to zero. In minimal groups, in-group favouritism appeared only as it rose with collective identification (interaction b = −.39); the in-group/out-group contrast was not significant (p = .07). | [NOTE-1246](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1246.md) | Cultural Trauma: Slavery and the Formation of African American Identity | The book's first chapter, read alone. Cultural trauma is a loss of identity and meaning in a group, not an individual wound, and need not be felt by everyone in it. Slavery became the trauma of African Americans "in retrospect": in the 1880s, when Reconstruction failed and white North and South reconciled around a memory of slavery as benign, a generation never enslaved made its memory the "primal scene" of a collective identity. Membership was set by "a common fate, not necessarily a common experience", whether or not one's ancestors were enslaved. Intellectuals and social movements carry the trauma; each social generation reworks it; it became national memory only with the civil rights movement. The chapter is a framework and a plan; the evidence is in chapters 2–6. | Read |
| [NOTE-1250](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1250.md) | Trauma, prejudice, large-group identity and psychoanalysis | A memorial lecture at the Freud Museum. Large-group identity is a tent's canvas worn over each person's individual identity, fixed in childhood through what parents deposit and unchangeable after adolescence. In two decades of unofficial dialogues, Volkan saw participants who felt their large-group identity threatened turn, with emotion, to an injury their ancestors suffered centuries ago. The shared image of such an event, real or mythologized, changes function across generations and becomes an identity marker: a chosen trauma. It feeds entitlement to recover what was lost and, in a "time collapse", makes the old event feel recent, as with Kosovo 1389 under Milošević. The Holocaust is not a chosen trauma: it is recent, its stories are alive, and it is mourned rather than kept as a wound for revenge. | Read |
| [NOTE-1251](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1251.md) | Self-categorization and social identification: Making sense of us and them | A textbook account of the social identity perspective. Self-categorization is hierarchical (personal, social, human) and situational (salience = accessibility × fit, with comparative and normative fit), and leads to depersonalization. Social identification has seven components (Ashmore et al. 2004). Social identity theory explains minimal-group bias by positive distinctiveness. Multiple-categorization models predict when bias falls. Unlike Hornsey 2008, it says the self-esteem hypothesis "has received extensive empirical support". | Read |
| [NOTE-1253](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1253.md) | Social Identity Theory and Self-categorization Theory: A Historical Review | A short critical history of the social identity approach. Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner 1979) is about intergroup relations: positive distinctiveness and the socio-structural variables of status, permeability, stability and legitimacy. Self-categorization theory (Turner et al. 1987) is about categorization at levels of inclusiveness, salience by accessibility and fit, and depersonalization. It records two dead ends (identification predicting bias, and the self-esteem hypothesis) and a later softening of the "functional antagonism" between personal and social identity. Hornsey lists the criticisms and declines to answer them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1256](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1256.md) | Identity fusion: The interplay of personal and social identities in extreme group behavior | Five preliminary studies and three two-wave experiments with Spanish students. A single pictorial item, the self as a small circle wholly inside a circle for Spain, picks out the "fused" (about 40%). Fusion is bimodal, related to but distinct from identification (r = .26 to .56) and specific to one group. The fused said they would fight and die for Spain more than others would. Activating their personal self, by challenging negative self-views or asking what they would fight for themselves, raised that willingness further; it did nothing for the nonfused. The authors read this as personal and social identity being "functionally equivalent" in the fused, against self-categorization theory's functional antagonism. | Read |
| [NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md) | Group-level self-definition and self-investment: A hierarchical (multicomponent) model of in-group identification | Seven studies with Dutch students. Identification has five components on two correlated dimensions (r = .61 to .77): self-definition (self-stereotyping, in-group homogeneity) and self-investment (solidarity, satisfaction, centrality). The model fit Dutch, European and university identification better than one-factor or cognitive-versus-affective models. Weeks to months later, the components predicted different reactions. Shown their group's mistreatment of Rwandan asylum seekers, those who saw themselves as like the average European felt more guilt, while those satisfied with being European, and for whom it was central, legitimized the policy. The self-circle overlap measure correlated with self-investment as much as with self-stereotyping. | Read |
| [NOTE-1266](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1266.md) | Being one of us. Group identification, joint actions, and collective intentionality | "Group identification", as philosophers of shared agency use it (Pacherie, Petersson), runs together two separable processes. One is adopting the group's perspective, asking "what should we do?". The other is self-transformation, coming to understand oneself as a member. The first can occur without the second (the discursive dilemma) and the second without the first (toddlers' joint action before age three). Self-transformation is not a belief but a Pushmi-Pullyu representation: "you are a member of us; act as such", at once describing and motivating, triggered by cues such as joint attention, and not under direct rational control. A conceptual paper. | Read |
| [NOTE-1268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1268.md) | Social Influence and Group Identity | A review of the group-identity account of social influence, grounded in self-categorization theory. Influence from a group need not be compliance for approval: when the group is a level of the self, in-group sources produce private acceptance, so influence is "partly self-influence". Classic conformity, obedience, minority-influence, emergency, helping and contagion findings are reread as bounded by shared identity. Identification, prototypicality, intergroup threat and context moderate the effect. Isolation and anonymity strengthen group influence, and crowd members switch to a group identity rather than losing the self. The evidence is reported, not presented. | Read |
| [NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md) | Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation | A theoretical review. Cultures construe the self as independent, bounded and defined by inner attributes (most clearly American), or as interdependent, defined by relationships with specific others in specific contexts (Japanese and other Asian, also African, Latin American, Hindu, southern European). For the interdependent self "others are included within the boundaries of the self", without "a merging of self and other". This is predicted to shape cognition (more knowledge of others, contextual self-description), emotion (other-focused over ego-focused emotions) and motivation (achievement for others, modesty over self-enhancement). | [NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md) | Empathy, Altruism, and Group Identification | Cialdini et al. said empathy-induced helping is due to self-other merging. May argued that no reading of "merging" is both coherent and explanatory. The authors read it as group identification. In empathizing with Y, X comes to conceive of Y as part of X's social self, so Y's welfare is constitutive of X's first-person plural welfare. This explains Batson's similarity-induced helping in the same way as minimal-group favouritism, and needs no belief in being two bodies, since identification is a Pushmi-Pullyu representation (Salice and Miyazono). Such helping is altruistic at the individual level and egoistic at the group level. The empirical rebuttal by Batson et al. (1997) is set aside as out of scope. | Read |
| [NOTE-1278](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1278.md) | Social Identity Theory's Self-Esteem Hypothesis: A Review and Some Suggestions for Clarification | A qualitative review of over 40 studies of social identity theory's self-esteem hypothesis: discrimination raises self-esteem (corollary 1) and low self-esteem motivates discrimination (corollary 2). The theory implies specific social state self-esteem, esteem for this group, now; most studies measured global personal trait self-esteem. Counting experiments, corollary 1 has 18 for and 13 against, corollary 2 has 7 for and 28 against, and one of eight full tests supports both. Nine studies find high personal self-esteem goes with the most discrimination. Discrimination seems to raise self-esteem without being motivated by a need for it, so the hypothesis fails "in its full and unqualified form". | [NOTE-1280](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1280.md) | Group Identity, Social Influence, and Collective Action Online: Extensions and Applications of the SIDE Model | The SIDE model as its authors state it. Deindividuation theory's account, in which anonymity and immersion cut self-awareness and release antinormative behaviour, is rejected. Anonymity within a group makes the salient identity more salient. With a group identity salient, people conform more to its local norms. With personal identity salient, they move away from the group norm. Depersonalization is "the emergence of group in the self", not a loss of self. A strategic dimension adds that anonymity to a powerful out-group frees in-group-normative behaviour it would punish. The model is extended to visible media, online communities and collective action. The evidence is reported, not presented. | Read |
| [NOTE-1284](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1284.md) | Self and Collective: Cognition and Social Context | Self-categorization theory's statement on the self. | [NOTE-1285](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1285.md) | Group-level emotions | A review of intergroup emotions theory by its founders. | [NOTE-1301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1301.md) | The Minimal Group Paradigm and its maximal impact in research on social categorization | A brief review of the minimal group paradigm. Groups are novel, arbitrary and anonymous, and allocations serve no personal interest. | [NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md) | Social identity theory | A textbook chapter. Social identity is the part of the self-concept that comes from group membership "together with the value or emotional significance attached to that membership" (Tajfel 1978). Categorization is always self-relevant, and the motive for a positive social identity drives comparison with out-groups; that identity serves needs for certainty, self-esteem and meaning. Low-status members choose individual mobility, collective action or social creativity by permeability, legitimacy and stability. Identification has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. At work, identification is said to matter more than "selfish concerns" of interdependence. An imagined common in-group raised children's helping of an immigrant classmate. | Read |
